lesson.title: Racing Toward Overkill: The Cold War Nuclear Arms Race
lesson.summary: The Soviet Union's surprise atomic bomb test in 1949 shattered America's nuclear monopoly and launched a decades long arms race in which both superpowers built ever more destructive weapons, eventually capable of destroying each other many times over.
lesson.body:
When the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, it possessed a weapon no other nation had, and American strategists assumed that monopoly would last for years, perhaps a decade. That confidence collapsed on August 29, 1949, when the Soviet Union successfully tested its own atomic bomb, years earlier than most American experts had predicted. Soviet scientists had been helped considerably by information stolen through espionage, but the test still came as a genuine shock in Washington, ending the sense of security the atomic monopoly had provided and deepening the fear that fueled the rise of McCarthyism that same year.

Truman's response was to push for an even more powerful weapon. In January 1950 he authorized development of the hydrogen bomb, a thermonuclear weapon that used a fission reaction to trigger a much larger fusion reaction, producing an explosion potentially hundreds of times more powerful than the bombs dropped on Japan. The United States tested its first hydrogen device, codenamed Ivy Mike, at Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific in November 1952, and the Soviet Union followed with a hydrogen bomb test of its own less than a year later, in August 1953, closing the gap even faster than it had with the atomic bomb.

From that point on, the two superpowers were locked in a continuous competition to build more, and more powerful, weapons and better ways of delivering them, including long range bombers and eventually intercontinental ballistic missiles. Neither side could afford to fall behind, because doing so might tempt the other into a first strike or dangerous political pressure, yet each new weapon built by one side only convinced the other to build more in response. By the late 1950s both nations possessed arsenals large enough to devastate each other many times over, a condition strategists eventually called mutual assured destruction, in which neither side could rationally launch a nuclear war because both sides would be destroyed. This same competition in rocket technology, since missiles built to deliver nuclear warheads relied on much of the same engineering as rockets meant for space, set the stage for the next great Cold War rivalry: the Space Race.
